original_value: This study investigates math anxiety (MA) by comparing trait-components of MA with real-time assessments of situational anxiety responses (state-components) in children. The research to date on MA in children is somewhat disparate in regard to methodology, and firm conclusions regarding the relation of MA to intelligence, math achievement and learning motivation are not readily drawn. Typically, the measures used in the MA research have differed by operationalizing either trait-MA and/or state- (or statelike)-MA, but have failed to compare the implications of their respective assumptions and the significance of their findings. Trait-MA and state-MA, self-ratings of math skills, attitudes towards mathematics, math achievement, the social anxiety, test anxiety, learning motivation and intelligence of 1,179 students (48.1% girls) from grades 4 and 5, were assessed. The findings yield evidence of a pronounced state-trait discrepancy. A negative correlation between state-MA and math achievement was observed for all intelligence levels, even when controlling for test- and social-anxiety traits, while there was no negative relation between trait-MA and achievement. State-MA was associated with lower intelligence, lower self-ratings, more negative attitudes, higher performance avoidance and work avoidance goals. In contrast, trait-MA was slightly related to higher mastery approach goals. The failure to adequately differentiate between state- and trait-based research into MA appears to be one reason for key inconsistencies between research findings and warrants further investigations.

result.paraphrase: This study examines math anxiety (MA) by contrasting trait-based components of MA with real-time ratings of situational anxiety responses (state components) in children. Prior research on MA in children has been somewhat inconsistent methodologically, so firm conclusions about how MA relates to intelligence, math achievement, and learning motivation are not easily drawn. In general, MA studies have used measures that operationalize either trait MA and/or state (or state-like) MA, yet they have not compared the implications of these underlying assumptions or the meaning of their results. Trait MA and state MA, self-ratings of math ability, attitudes toward mathematics, math achievement, social anxiety, test anxiety, learning motivation, and intelligence were assessed in 1,179 students in grades 4 and 5 (48.1% girls). The results provide evidence of a pronounced discrepancy between state and trait. State MA showed a negative correlation with math achievement across all intelligence levels, even after controlling for test-anxiety and social-anxiety traits, whereas trait MA showed no negative association with achievement. State MA was linked to lower intelligence, lower self-ratings, more negative attitudes, and stronger performance-avoidance and work-avoidance goals. By contrast, trait MA was weakly associated with higher mastery-approach goals. The lack of clear differentiation between state- and trait-based MA research seems to underlie key inconsistencies in the findings and calls for further study.
